Stiffened
STIF-und
v. (past of stiffen; made rigid; hardened)
English stiff, Saxon stif, rigid, unbending. In 2 Chronicles 36:13 it renders the Hebrew qashah, to be hard, used with 'oreph, the neck.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

The last king of Judah is summed up in one sentence: “And he also rebelled against king Nebuchadnezzar, who had made him swear by God: but he stiffened his neck, and hardened his heart from turning unto the LORD God of Israel” (2 Chronicles 36:13). Zedekiah broke an oath sworn by God and would not be turned. The Chronicler's verdict is the dictionary's verdict. Note the order: the neck first, then the heart. The stiff neck is the outward refusal to bow the head; the hard heart is the inward refusal to feel. Scripture uses the image from Exodus onward of a people who will not take the yoke — an ox that will not bend its neck to the collar cannot be driven. And note who does the stiffening: he stiffened his neck. Judicial hardening by God is real (Exodus 9:12; Romans 9:18), but it never erases the sinner's own act. The chapter ends with the temple burned and the people carried to Babylon, and the Chronicler gives the reason without ambiguity: “till there was no remedy” (2 Chronicles 36:16). A neck stiffened long enough becomes a nation's grave.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828): STIFFENED, participle passive Made stiff or rigid; made less pliant or flexible.

STIFFENED, participle passive Made stiff.

STIFFEN, verb transitive To make stiff; to make less pliant or flexible.

2. To make torpid; as, stiffened with cold.

3. To make obstinate; as, to stiffen the neck.

STIFFEN, verb intransitive To become stiff; to become more rigid or less flexible.

Key Scripture

2Ch 36:13 — "but he stiffened his neck, and hardened his heart from turning unto the LORD God of Israel."

2Ch 36:16 — "But they mocked the messengers of God, and despised his words, and misused his prophets, until the wrath of the LORD arose against his people, till there was no remedy."

Pro 29:1 — "He, that being often reproved hardeneth his neck, shall suddenly be destroyed, and that without remedy."

Modern Corruption

Hardening is now treated as damage done to a man; Scripture treats it here as a man's own act, and judicially righteous.

expand to see more

The therapeutic reading makes a hard heart a wound — something that happened to Zedekiah rather than something Zedekiah did. The Chronicler will not have it. He stiffened his neck; he hardened his heart; he broke an oath sworn by God. Sin is the category, not injury, and the remedy is repentance, not recovery.

The principle to recover is Proverbs 29:1. Reproof refused does not leave a man where he was; it leaves him harder. There is a point at which the Chronicler records no remedy — not because God's mercy ran out, but because the neck would not bend. That is a warning to be preached, not softened.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

From Saxon stif, rigid; renders Hebrew qashah with 'oreph, to make the neck hard, at 2 Chronicles 36:13.

expand to see more

Saxon stif, rigid, unbending.

Hebrew qashah, to be hard or severe; with 'oreph, the back of the neck.

The figure is an ox refusing the yoke on its neck.

2 Chronicles 36:13 is the only place the Authorized Version uses stiffened.

Zedekiah broke an oath sworn by God and would not turn.

Usage

"he stiffened his neck"

"hardened his heart from turning unto the LORD"

"till there was no remedy"
